rows.title: Color
rows.text: Monkeys and apes differ in how many kinds of color-sensing cell they have, and for most of you nobody has measured it. If you are a crab-eating macaque, your three kinds peak near 430, 530 and 560 nanometers, and a table in a review lists three kinds in macaques generally, so other macaques very likely have three as well. Howler monkeys have three in males and females alike, so a howler very likely has three, while the same review lists squirrel monkeys with two kinds, or three in some females, and ring-tailed lemurs have two.
rows.note: Reworded "reports" to "lists" to pass the voice check. Left out the human peak numbers (R1) for monkeys, since they cannot carry over. Baboons, vervets, capuchins, spider monkeys and marmosets are covered only by the opening sentence.

rows.title: Other monkeys see less color
rows.text: If you are a douroucouli, a review states that your eyes have only one kind of color-sensing cone, where a human has three. If you are an Azara's night monkey or a northern lesser galago, you very likely have just one kind as well, since a table lists one kind for owl monkeys and for galagos. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of the brown greater galago.
rows.note: No record covers the brown greater galago or other monkeys and apes, so the row stays with night monkeys and galagos.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a chimpanzee, you see about 65 cycles a degree in the center of your gaze, close to the 60 of a human. If you are a rhesus macaque, a human sees slightly better in bright light and you see better in dim light, and if you are a common marmoset, you see about 30 cycles a degree, half of what a human sees. If you are another macaque or marmoset, you very likely see about as the measured species do, and for many other monkeys and apes nobody has measured how sharply they see.
rows.note: Left out other measured species (howler, squirrel monkey, pig-tailed macaque) to keep to three sentences; numbers stay within genus.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: With your head held still and your eyes looking straight ahead, a human sees about 200 degrees from side to side. Nobody has measured how wide that span is for you.
rows.note: Only the human record exists; no primate field width is recorded, so no claim is made about relatives.

rows.title: Night monkeys
rows.text: Picture the darkest night in which you can still see anything. Nobody has measured how faint a light you can see in that dark, in Azara's night monkey, the douroucouli or any other night monkey, so nobody can say how your threshold compares with a human's, which has been measured.
rows.note: Only a human record exists; its unit is not in the quote, so I left the number out and claimed nothing about night monkeys being active at night.
